newsitem.title: FRANCE: Focus - Three bids for Air Liberte, Virgin interested.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Three bids for Air Liberte, Virgin interested.

text.p: Two French groups have submitted proposals to take over insolvent carrier Air Liberte, providing domestic alternatives to a bid unveiled on Monday by British Airways, a French court official said on Tuesday.

A French consortium led by travel company Nouvelles Frontieres that includes Royal Air Maroc, and another group led by pilot Fernand Danan, representing the staff of airline AOM, submitted proposals on Monday, said Gilles Baronnie, a judicial administrator appointed by the Creteil commercial court.
Baronnie said Richard Branson's Virgin Express had confirmed it was interested in Air Liberte, which went into receivership on September 26, but had not submitted an offer.

Although Monday was the deadline for offers, Baronnie said the court would be willing to study any proposal from Virgin in addition to the three firm offers to run the insolvent French airline with its precious landing slots at Paris's Orly airport.
British Airways announced on Monday that it was offering 25 million francs to buy Air Liberte, undeterred by reports that French authorities would prefer a French buyer.
The British carrier said it believed it could revive Air Liberte by merging it with its own French subsidiary TAT and would preserve 1,250 Air Liberte jobs out of around 1,400.

Nouvelles Frontieres chairman Jacques Maillot, who also heads the charter company Corsair, said he had assembled a consortium with both the financial clout and operational know-how through Royal Air Maroc to rescue Air Liberte.
"Our objective is to create a big private company, which would be independent and competitive against Air France and other European and international rivals," Maillot told Radio Classique.
State-owned Air France's domestic arm, Air France Europe, dominates the French market.
"It's clear that Air France prefers Nouvelles Frontieres to British Airways, and everyone knows I have good relations with (Air France chairman) Christian Blanc," Maillot said.
But he denied British Airways' charge that he had been asked to put in a bid. "I was not solicited by the authorities. I took the initiative myself," Maillot said.
In addition to Royal Air Maroc, which confirmed that it was involved in a bid for Air Liberte, the consortium includes Financiere Moncey, a subsidiary of the Groupe Rivaud bank.

The newspaper Les Echos said Groupe Rivaud, the leading shareholder in Air Liberte, would keep 75 to 80 percent of the airline under the plan. Air Maroc would have 10-15 percent, and Nouvelles Frontieres around 10 percent.
The group proposes a rescue plan, rather than a buyout, and would run Air Liberte as a business rather than to absorb it through a merger.

Maillot reiterated that the group would seek in a second stage to acquire AOM, formerly Air Outre-Mer, one of the assets of state bank Credit Lyonnais that is slated to be sold as part of a state bailout of the bank.
He said he was in talks with the Consortium de Realisation, the agency grouping Credit Lyonnais assets to be sold.
TAT chairman Marc Rochet declined to say whether British Airways would also bid for AOM, but Maillot said that was the British group's objective.
Baronnie said the third offer, led by AOM pilot Danan, proposed a 120 million franc buyout, but he said he had not examined the financing or details.
The court has six months to study the offers, but officials expect a decision soon given the airline's precarious condition.
BA's offer is good to October 30.
Air Liberte, which owns around a quarter of the slots at Orly, lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996 and has 1.5 billion francs of debt.
Air Liberte, AOM, Eurolair, BA's TAT and other carriers have been hurt by a price war aimed at increasing market share ahead of the liberalisation of the European air market in 1997.
